item.title: Day 5 of the short Odissey
item.dc:creator: Eva Rogelj
item.description:
Gigi plot this table!

Today we learned about ggplot. The ggplot2 library is something that many are now already familiar with. I have recently found the tidyplots library [Quarto] (https://tidyplots.org/). It’s very nice as it builds on top of ggplot.

One most important thing I have learned today was how to introduce a break into my y-axis. I can do that using the ggbreak library.

library(ggbreak)
ggbreak v0.1.7 Learn more at https://yulab-smu.top/
If you use ggbreak in published research, please cite the following
paper:

S Xu, M Chen, T Feng, L Zhan, L Zhou, G Yu. Use ggbreak to effectively
utilize plotting space to deal with large datasets and outliers.
Frontiers in Genetics. 2021, 12:774846. doi: 10.3389/fgene.2021.774846
ggplot(merged_filtered %>% filter(Epitope %in% c("NANP5", "NPDP")),
       aes(x = factor(Timepoint), y = normalised, fill = Epitope)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Timepoint",
    y = "Normalised ED50",
    title = "Plasma antibody titres"
  ) +
  theme_prism() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    text = element_text(size = 14)
  ) +
  scale_y_break(breaks = c(10000, 20000), scales = 1, space = 1)

ggsave(
  filename = paste0(figures.dir, "boxplots_axis_break.png"),
  width = 6, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300
)

item.title: Day 4 of the 5-day Odissey
item.dc:creator: Eva Rogelj
item.description:
Day 4: Pipelines - the horror: nf-core

nfcore introduction

Nf-core is a very active community around nextflow. Volunteers develop nextflow pipelines around a variety of bioinformatic data. Nf-core link

All nf-core pipelines are open source and the source code is available on github. The pipelines are developed by volunteers, who can have a very varied background.

A standard one that we tried first is rnaseq: rnaseq

But one applicable to my research if airrflow: airrflow

Using an nf-core pipeline: Set pixi environment

#| eval: false
pixi init nextflow_test -c conda-forge -c bioconda

Add nf-core and nextflow

#| eval: false
pixi add nextflow nf-core

Can check if it worked by:

#| eval: false
pixi run nextflow -version
pixi run nf-core --help
pixi run nextflow run hello

You need a configuration file

#| eval: false
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hpc2n/intro-course/master/exercises/NEXTFLOW/INTERACTIVE/hpc2n.config
#| eval: false
// Config profile for HPC2N
params {
  config_profile_description = 'Cluster profile for HPC2N'
  config_profile_contact = 'Pedro Ojeda @pojeda'
  config_profile_url = 'https://www.hpc2n.umu.se/'
  project = null
  clusterOptions = null
  max_memory = 128.GB
  max_cpus = 28
  max_time = 168.h
  email = 'pedroojeda2011@gmail.com'
}

singularity {
  enabled = true
}

process {
  executor = 'slurm'
  clusterOptions = { "-A $params.project ${params.clusterOptions ?: ''}" }
}

I ran the test data with airrflow

#| eval: false
nextflow run nf-core/airrflow -r 5.1.1 -profile test --outdir <OUTDIR>

item.title: Day 3 of the 5-day Odyssey
item.dc:creator: Eva Rogelj
item.description:
Day 3: Nextflow! Finally, no more running one script after another by hand.

Why a workflow manager? Oh Why?

In bioinformatics you usually end up with one script per tool, and you run them one by one. That whole chain is a workflow (or pipeline). It gets old fast, especially with lots of samples that all need different amounts of compute.

A workflow manager turns your scripts into one automated pipeline. One command and it:

  • runs everything in the right order
  • keeps an eye on the jobs
  • moves files between steps
  • re-runs whatever failed

Bonus: pipelines are portable, reproducible, easier to install (especially with containers) and don’t waste time between steps.

There are two big ones, Snakemake and Nextflow. We’re doing Nextflow.

Nextflow in a nutshell

  • Scripts become processes, connected by channels (the data flowing in and out).
  • The workflow block says what runs in which order.
  • A process can run any language, so you can reuse old scripts.
  • Same pipeline on a laptop, an HPC cluster or the cloud. Only the config changes.
  • Works with git and containers (Apptainer, Docker).
  • Develop on a few samples, then scale to hundreds.
  • If something breaks, it can resume from the failed step instead of starting over.

A process looks roughly like this (pseudo-code, don’t run it):

process PROCESS_NAME {
    container
    input:
      data x
    script:
      task1
      task2
    output:
      output x
}

First workflow

Start from a pixi environment (see Day 2):

#| eval: false
pixi init -c conda-forge -c bioconda

Then put this in hello.nf:

#!/usr/bin/env nextflow

params.greeting = 'Hello world!'

process SPLITLETTERS {
    input:
    val x

    output:
    path 'chunk_*'

    script:
    """
    printf '$x' | split -b 6 - chunk_
    """
}

process CONVERTTOUPPER {
    input:
    path y

    output:
    stdout

    script:
    """
    cat $y | tr '[a-z]' '[A-Z]'
    """
}

workflow {
    greeting_ch = Channel.of(params.greeting)
    letters_ch = SPLITLETTERS(greeting_ch)
    results_ch = CONVERTTOUPPER(letters_ch.flatten())
    results_ch.view{ it }
}
#| eval: false
pixi run nextflow run hello.nf

Output (the order can flip, because the two CONVERTTOUPPER tasks run at the same time):

executor >  local (3)
[96/fd5f07] SPLITLETTERS (1)   [100%] 1 of 1 ✔
[7e/dad424] CONVERTTOUPPER (2) [100%] 2 of 2 ✔
HELLO
WORLD!

Changed something small and don’t want to redo everything? Add -resume:

#| eval: false
pixi run nextflow run hello.nf -resume

Parameters live under params. (like params.greeting) and can be overridden on the command line with --greeting.

To check and clean up old runs:

#| eval: false
pixi run nextflow log
pixi run nextflow clean -f
pixi run nextflow clean -before <RUN NAME> -f

The RNA-seq pipeline

Three tools:

  • Salmon: quantifies transcripts from RNA-seq reads
  • FastQC: quality control of the raw reads
  • MultiQC: collects all the logs into one HTML report

And the order makes sense once you see why:

  1. Index the transcriptome (salmon index). Salmon needs a searchable index, not a plain FASTA. Done once, reused by every sample.
  2. Quantify (salmon quant). Maps each read pair against the index and estimates how much of each transcript is there.
  3. FastQC. Runs alongside quantification, since QC doesn’t depend on the counting.
  4. MultiQC. Waits for everything, then gives one report instead of dozens of files.

Config

Everything about where the pipeline runs goes in nextflow.config:

process {
    executor = 'slurm'
    time = 2.h
    cpus = 4
}

resume = true
singularity.enabled = true

executor {
    account = 'your_project_account'
}

So: everything goes to slurm, resume is always on (no more -resume), Singularity is enabled for containers, and the account is whatever your allocation ID is. Nextflow finds this file by itself as long as you run from the same folder.

Parameters

script1.nf:

#!/usr/bin/env nextflow

params.reads = "$projectDir/data/ggal/gut_{1,2}.fq"
params.transcriptome_file = "$projectDir/data/ggal/transcriptome.fa"
params.multiqc = "$projectDir/multiqc"

workflow {
    println "reads: $params.reads"
}
#| eval: false
pixi run nextflow run script1.nf

Index the transcriptome

A process has an input, an output and a script. Add this to script1.nf (already in script2.nf):

process INDEX {
    input:
    path transcriptome

    output:
    path 'salmon_index'

    script:
    """
    salmon index --threads $task.cpus -t $transcriptome -i salmon_index
    """
}

and swap the workflow block for:

workflow {
    index_ch = INDEX(file(params.transcriptome_file, checkIfExists: true))
}

Run it and… it fails. What did we forget? Salmon isn’t installed yet. Two options:

A. Add it to the environment

#| eval: false
pixi add salmon

B. Use a container (more reproducible). Add this inside the process, above input:

container 'oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/salmon:2.7.0--cb05356ce9eb88b7'
Note

You can also give a process its own output folder, just under container:

publishDir "$params.outdir/salmon"

By default it links files into work/, which is fast but the files vanish if you clean work/. Add mode: 'copy' for results you want to keep.

Resources per process

In nextflow.config, inside the process block (before its closing brace):

withName: 'INDEX' {
    time = 15.m
    cpus = 2
}

Need memory? Add something like memory = 8.GB. Here 2 CPUs come with enough, so I skipped it.

Quick detour: tuples

Salmon needs both reads of a pair together. The data folder has six files (three samples, two each):

gut_1.fq    gut_2.fq
liver_1.fq  liver_2.fq
lung_1.fq   lung_2.fq

fromFilePairs groups them for us (script3.nf). The {1,2} marks the part that’s allowed to differ:

workflow {
    read_pairs_ch = channel.fromFilePairs(params.reads)
    read_pairs_ch.view()
}

Each item is a tuple: the sample ID plus the list of its two files.

[gut, [/.../data/ggal/gut_1.fq, /.../data/ggal/gut_2.fq]]

Think matching socks: _1 and _2 get paired by their shared name. params.reads only points at gut, so to see all three:

#| eval: false
pixi run nextflow run script3.nf --reads 'data/ggal/*_{1,2}.fq'

Quantification

script4.nf adds QUANTIFICATION. It takes two inputs: the index_ch from before, and the read pairs tuple (sample_id plus reads).

#| eval: false
pixi run nextflow run script4.nf
pixi run nextflow run script4.nf --reads 'data/ggal/*_{1,2}.fq'

With more files, QUANTIFICATION just runs multiple times in parallel. That’s Nextflow doing its thing.

FastQC

Same idea, same input as QUANTIFICATION.

MultiQC

Last step: collect the outputs of QUANTIFICATION and FASTQC into a report. What do you need to think about here?

We want one MultiQC task and one report, so it has to wait for everything else. Combine the channels with mix, then collect them into a single element:

MULTIQC(quant_ch.mix(fastqc_ch).collect())

:::

item.title: Day 2 of the 5-day Odyssey
item.dc:creator: Eva Rogelj
item.description:
Day 2: Setting up an environment

Today we talked about reproducible environments with Pixi.

Installing Pixi

wget -qO- https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh

Creating an environment

Run this once in the folder you’re working in:

pixi init name_pixi_training -c conda-forge -c bioconda

This creates a pixi.toml file, which looks something like this:

1[workspace]
2channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"]
3name = "name_pixi_training"
4platforms = ["linux-64"]
version = "0.1.0"

5[tasks]

6[dependencies]
1
Overview section of the environment.
2
Channels: the sources we allow our tools and dependencies to come from.
3
The name of the environment.
4
The operating system the environment is optimised for.
5
Where tasks can be defined
6
The list of tools installed in the environment.

The lock file

pixi.lock record of the channels and package source, license information, md5 checksums, and more.

Important

Do not delete the pixi.toml or pixi.lock files. It breaks the environment, which will make you sad :(

Using the environment

Add a dependency with add:

pixi add quarto

Enter the environment:

pixi shell

Leave it again with:

exit

item.title: Day 1 of the 5-day Odyssey
item.dc:creator: Eva Rogelj
item.description:
Day 1: only beginning to dream about being a bioinformatician

Today was all about data management and reproducible research: the habits that make an analysis something you (and others) can trust and repeat.

FAIR principles

Data should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. The FAIR principles rely on good data management in every phase of research:

  • Research documentation
  • Data organisation
  • Information security
  • Ethics and legislation

Best practices for file organisation

  • Keep a folder for the raw data, and never alter it.
  • Keep code separate from data.
  • Use a version control system (at least for code), e.g. git.
  • Put a README in every directory describing its purpose and contents.
  • Use file naming schemes that make files easy to find and understand, for humans and machines, and document them.
  • Use non-proprietary formats: .csv rather than .xlsx.

Literate programming

  • Document your methods and workflows.
  • Document where and when you downloaded data.
  • Document the versions of the software you ran.

Git cheat sheet

Here are some git commands worth keeping handy.

Getting started

git clone https://github.com/username/repo.git   # clone a repo

Basic workflow

git status                    # see what changed
git add .                     # stage all changes
git commit -m "message"       # commit with a message
git push                      # push to GitHub
git pull                      # pull the latest changes

Branches

git branch                    # list branches
git branch new-branch         # create a new branch
git checkout new-branch       # switch to a branch
git checkout -b new-branch    # create and switch in one go
git push origin new-branch    # push the branch to GitHub

Undoing changes

git restore filename          # undo changes to a file
git reset HEAD~1              # undo last commit (keep changes)
git revert HEAD               # undo last commit (by creating a new commit)

Viewing history

git log                       # see commits
git log --oneline             # shorter view
git diff                      # see what changed

Merging branches

git checkout main             # switch to main
git merge new-branch          # merge the branch into main

Stashing (temporary save)

git stash                     # save changes temporarily
git stash pop                 # restore them
